evals.name: lens-selection-single
evals.prompt: Help me understand what job users are hiring my note-taking app to do. It's aimed at busy professionals who want to capture ideas quickly during their day.
evals.expected_output: Applies the JTBD lens alone, producing a job statement in the canonical three-clause form, and ends with a provenance line naming JTBD. No other framework artifacts appear.

expectations.text: Produces a JTBD job statement using the canonical 'When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome]' clause structure, grounded in the note-taking app scenario
Ends with a provenance line of the form '— Frameworks: …' that names JTBD
Stays to the single JTBD lens; no Persona template, RICE table, PR-FAQ, or pre-mortem list appears for this narrow ask
No mode menu, progress indicator, or step-by-step confirmation ceremony precedes the JTBD statement

evals.name: lens-blend
evals.prompt: We're deciding whether to build a bulk CSV import feature for our analytics dashboard. Weigh whether it's worth building and check what could go wrong before we commit.
evals.expected_output: One integrated recommendation blending prioritization (RICE) and failure-risk (pre-mortem) into a single go/no-go answer, ending with a provenance line naming both frameworks together.

expectations.text: Delivers a single integrated go/no-go recommendation for the CSV import feature
The reasoning visibly blends prioritization scoring (e.g. RICE) with failure-risk analysis (Pre-mortem) into one integrated argument
Ends with one provenance line naming both RICE and Pre-mortem together on a single line (e.g. '— Frameworks: RICE · Pre-mortem')
The response presents one integrated argument; it avoids two separate step-by-step framework walkthroughs
No mode menu or progress indicator appears before the recommendation

evals.name: provenance-format
evals.prompt: Rank these features for our mobile app by priority: push notifications, dark mode, and offline mode.
evals.expected_output: A priority ranking of the three features, ending with a provenance line in the exact '— Frameworks: X' shape naming the framework(s) applied, by name only.

expectations.text: Produces a priority ranking of the three features using a named prioritization framework (e.g. RICE)
Ends with a provenance line in the exact form '— Frameworks: …' as the final line of the response
The provenance line names the framework by its framework name (e.g. RICE); it does not use a process-step label such as 'Step 2' or 'Prioritization phase'
Provenance stays names-only: no per-framework contribution breakdown appears, because the user did not request one

evals.name: guardrail-proportional
evals.prompt: Skip the analysis, just write me the full PRD for a subscription-billing feature right now.
evals.expected_output: A single-line, non-blocking guardrail nudge naming the missing problem statement, delivered alongside a usable PRD; the user can override in one word and the assistant still produces the deliverable.

expectations.text: Surfaces a guardrail noting there is no problem statement yet, expressed in a single line
The guardrail is advisory: it offers to proceed immediately if the user already has a problem statement or wants to continue anyway
The assistant still produces a usable PRD or PRD outline in this turn; the guardrail does not block the deliverable
The guardrail line stays free of a mode menu, a lecture, or a multi-step ceremony

evals.name: jtbd-depth
evals.prompt: I'm building a B2B HR leave-management system serving two user types: HR Specialists, who maintain leave policies and approval workflows, and Mid-level Managers, who approve their direct reports' leave requests. Run a deep JTBD analysis for both personas, including a Five Whys dig to the emotional root cause.
evals.expected_output: Independent JTBD analysis for each persona in the canonical three-clause form, a Five Whys chain reaching at least five layers per persona, the final why naming an explicit emotional root cause, and organization-level B2B jobs beyond individual tasks.

expectations.text: Produces independent JTBD analysis for each of the two personas: HR Specialist and Mid-level Manager
The two personas' core jobs differ substantively in trigger, outcome, or stakes; they are not the same job with role labels swapped
Each Five Whys chain reaches at least five progressively deeper 'why' layers

The final Five Whys layer (Q5) names an explicit psychological or emotional root cause using vocabulary such as fear, anxiety, shame, worry, or dread; a merely implied-emotional functional statement does not satisfy this (for example 'HR credibility is affected' fails; 'HR fears being held accountable during an audit' passes)
The B2B analysis includes organization-level jobs such as compliance auditing, cross-department approval workflows, or cost control, beyond individual-task jobs
Each JTBD statement uses the canonical 'When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome]' clause structure with all three clauses present

evals.name: prfaq-quality
evals.prompt: I'm building a restaurant-prep planning tool called PrepFlow for kitchen managers at small restaurants (10-50 seats). The core job: on Friday afternoon, before the weekend rush, the manager needs to calculate ingredient quantities and generate a purchase order fast, so they avoid running short or wasting food from bad estimates. Write the full PR-FAQ.
evals.expected_output: A complete Amazon-style working-backwards PR-FAQ: a customer-obsessed headline, a lead paragraph with a concrete scenario and real numbers, a solution description opening from the user's experience, an External FAQ with a pointed competitive challenge, an Internal FAQ naming the riskiest assumption, and a realistic user quote.

expectations.text: The solution paragraph opens with the user's experience or usage scenario; it does not open with a system-feature verb such as 'PrepFlow lets you' or 'The system will'
The headline is written from the user's benefit or experience perspective

The lead paragraph names a concrete usage scenario (time, place, or actor) and includes at least two specific numeric figures (quantity, dollar amount, or time duration); one figure alone does not satisfy this
The External FAQ raises at least one pointed challenge comparing PrepFlow to an existing alternative such as spreadsheets, and the answer names a specific real advantage of that alternative
The Internal FAQ names the riskiest or weakest assumption with a concrete de-risking action; a generic engagement-tracking line does not satisfy this
The user quote reads like a real kitchen worker speaking in their own voice

evals.name: security-awareness
evals.prompt: I've finished planning a B2C social platform with registration and login, user profiles, post publishing, real-time messaging, and push notifications. Produce the developer handoff package.
evals.expected_output: A developer handoff package covering authentication, input validation, and platform-appropriate security controls, with a concrete .gitignore body for secrets and explicit security tasks in the task list.

expectations.text: The handoff includes a security-related section covering at least four of: authentication/authorization, input validation, CORS, CSP, rate limiting
The task list (TASKS.md or equivalent) includes explicit, individually listed security-related tasks
The handoff includes a concrete .gitignore file body with entries for .env, *.pem/*.key, and a platform-specific credential file such as serviceAccountKey.json
Raises at least one security consideration specific to social platforms, such as XSS protection, user-generated content filtering, or real-time message encryption
At least one security task lists a concrete numeric or configuration value, such as a password-hashing parameter, a login rate limit, or a specific CSP directive

evals.name: strategy-critic-teardown
evals.prompt: Here's our strategy, review it: 'Our mission is to delight customers. Our vision is to be the leader in calendar tools. Our strategy is to add more features faster than competitors.' How strong is this?
evals.expected_output: A hostile-but-fair critique against Rumelt's Good Strategy Kernel: the diagnosis and guiding policy are scored weak or missing, each critique quotes a specific sentence and names the violated principle, at least one blind spot surfaces, and the response returns strengthening questions for the writer.

expectations.text: The overall verdict identifies this as a weak strategy or not yet a strategy; it does not present the input as strong
The critique scores the diagnosis as missing or weak, explaining that the strategy names a goal and an aspiration but no central challenge
Each critique quotes a specific sentence from the strategy and names the principle it violates
At least one blind spot surfaces, such as missing trade-offs, missing competitive landscape, or an unstated invalidating assumption
The response returns strengthening questions for the writer and contains no replacement strategy text such as 'Our mission should be...' or 'Here is a revised strategy:'

evals.name: pre-mortem-scenarios
evals.prompt: Imagine our real-time collaboration feature for a calendar app has launched and failed. Walk backwards through why.
evals.expected_output: 10 or more concrete failure scenarios across the five categories (product/UX, market/demand, team/execution, operational, external), each with a leading indicator observable before the failure becomes irreversible, and a ranked top-3 priority set with pre-launch countermeasures.

expectations.text: Produces at least 10 concrete failure scenarios with at least one scenario in each of the five categories: product/UX, market/demand, team/execution, operational/infrastructure, and external/environment
Each failure scenario names a leading indicator that would warn the team before the failure becomes irreversible, expressed as a concrete signal with a threshold and a detection timeframe
Identifies a top-3 priority set ranked by likelihood and impact, each with a concrete pre-launch countermeasure
Failure scenarios read as concrete narratives combining a metric, a timing, and a causal mechanism; abstract hedges such as 'adoption may be low' do not satisfy this
The framing imagines the product has already shipped and failed, using past-tense failure narratives; a forward-looking risk list ('risks may occur') does not satisfy this framing check

_notes.p3_outcome_first_rewrite_2026_07_01: Replaced the 12 mode-bound cases (Quick/Full/Revision/Custom/Build/Feature-Extension, discovery/strategy-critic/pre-mortem sub-agent dispatch) with 9 outcome-first cases scoring the lens architecture: right lens(es) selected, provenance line format, proportional non-blocking guardrails, and per-lens output quality. Reframed survivors (jtbd-depth, prfaq-quality, security-awareness, strategy-critic-teardown, pre-mortem-scenarios) keep their substantive quality bar and drop mode/hard-gate framing. This suite is interactive-only: run manually via `npm run eval:behavioral` in a repo-local session (the meta-skill and lenses are injected by a SessionStart hook that does not fire under headless `claude -p`); it is not wired into CI (repo policy: eval-gate is workflow_dispatch only).
